claim: Force transduction at cell-cell adhesions regulates tissue development, maintenance and adaptation.
source: Force transduction at cell-cell adhesions regulates tissue development, maintenance and adaptation.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding of tissue mechanics.

claim: Basal force fluctuations were coupled to E-cadherin localization at the level of individual cell-cell junctions.
source: Applying this technology to spontaneously-forming adherent epithelial cell clusters, we found that basal force fluctuations were coupled to E-cadherin localization at the level of individual cell-cell junctions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the correlation analyses shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Cell-cell force exchange depended on the cell position within a cluster.
source: At the multi-cellular scale, cell-cell force exchange depended on the cell position within a cluster, and was adaptive to reconfigurations due to cell divisions or positional rearrangements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7, which categorizes forces by cell connectivity (k).

claim: Force transmission through a cell required coordinated modulation of cell-matrix adhesion and actomyosin contractility in the cell and its neighbors.
source: Importantly, force transmission through a cell required coordinated modulation of cell-matrix adhesion and actomyosin contractility in the cell and its neighbors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from perturbation experiments shown in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for tissue morphogenesis during development.
source: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for diverse multi-cellular processes, including tissue morphogenesis during development (Mammoto and Ingber, 2010; Martin et al., 2010; Rauzi et al., 2010; Lecuit et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for collective migration during wound healing.
source: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for diverse multi-cellular processes, including tissue morphogenesis during development (Mammoto and Ingber, 2010; Martin et al., 2010; Rauzi et al., 2010; Lecuit et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2012), collective migration during wound healing (Trepat et al., 2009; Tambe et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for epithelial and endothelial barrier functions.
source: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for diverse multi-cellular processes, including tissue morphogenesis during development (Mammoto and Ingber, 2010; Martin et al., 2010; Rauzi et al., 2010; Lecuit et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2012), collective migration during wound healing (Trepat et al., 2009; Tambe et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012), epithelial and endothelial barrier functions (Tzima et al., 2005; Twiss et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for cancer progression.
source: The importance of mechanical coupling between cells has been documented for diverse multi-cellular processes, including tissue morphogenesis during development (Mammoto and Ingber, 2010; Martin et al., 2010; Rauzi et al., 2010; Lecuit et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2012), collective migration during wound healing (Trepat et al., 2009; Tambe et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2012), epithelial and endothelial barrier functions (Tzima et al., 2005; Twiss et al., 2012), and cancer progression (Friedl et al., 2004; Bajpai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The method utilizes high-resolution traction force microscopy (TFM) and time-lapse live cell microscopy to quantify cell-cell mechanical interactions.
source: We developed a method that utilizes high-resolution traction force microscopy (TFM) and time-lapse live cell microscopy to quantify cell–cell mechanical interactions in dynamic multi-cellular clusters
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology developed and used in the study.

claim: The method provides sub-cellular resolution needed to measure force exchange at the level of individual junctions.
source: We developed a method that utilizes high-resolution traction force microscopy (TFM) and time-lapse live cell microscopy to quantify cell–cell mechanical interactions in dynamic multi-cellular clusters, while maintaining the sub-cellular resolution needed to measure force exchange at the level of individual junctions.
evidence: This describes a capability of the developed method, validated by the data in Figure 6.

claim: Previous studies inferred cell-cell force transmission from the regional imbalance of traction forces in cell pairs and three-cell clusters in linear configurations.
source: Our method expanded upon several pioneering studies, which inferred cell–cell force transmission from the regional imbalance of traction forces in cell pairs and three-cell clusters in linear configurations (Liu et al., 2010; Maruthamuthu et al., 2011; McCain et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim references previous work in the field.

claim: The thin-plate modeling approach of cells and finite element analysis was utilized by other studies to infer intercellular interactions in entire cell sheets.
source: To achieve reconstruction of forces at individual cell–cell junctions and in cell clusters of generic configurations, we incorporated the thin-plate modeling approach of cells and finite element analysis of the plate deformation that was utilized by other studies to infer intercellular interactions in entire cell sheets (Trepat et al., 2009; Tambe et al., 2011, 2013; Hur et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim references previous methodological work.

claim: The spatial distributions and dynamics of basal cell-cell force transmission correlated with morphogenetic events such as cell divisions.
source: Our results revealed that the spatial distributions and dynamics of basal cell–cell force transmission correlated with morphogenetic events such as cell divisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Local mechanical stresses correlated with localization of E-cadherin molecules along the cell junction.
source: Along the cell junction, we showed with sub-interface resolution that the local mechanical stresses also correlated with localization of E-cadherin molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Force propagation through cells can be intercepted by cell anchorage to the extracellular matrix.
source: Expanding our approach to temporal force fluctuation analysis at the length scale of a cell, we found that force propagation through cells can be intercepted by cell anchorage to the extracellular matrix and by actomyosin contraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from perturbation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Force propagation through cells can be intercepted by actomyosin contraction.
source: Expanding our approach to temporal force fluctuation analysis at the length scale of a cell, we found that force propagation through cells can be intercepted by cell anchorage to the extracellular matrix and by actomyosin contraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from perturbation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Traction forces exerted by a single cell or by a cluster of cells are in mechanical equilibrium with the extracellular substrate.
source: The principle states that traction forces exerted by a single cell, or by a cluster of cells, are in mechanical equilibrium with the extracellular substrate.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of mechanics applied to cells.

claim: The traction forces integrated over the footprint of a single cell or a cell cluster must be equal to zero.
source: Hence, the traction forces integrated over the footprint of a single cell or a cell cluster must be equal to zero (Figure 1; see 'The force-balancing principle and its application to larger cell clusters' in 'Materials and methods' section).
evidence: This follows from the principle of mechanical equilibrium.

claim: If the integrated traction force over the footprint of an individual cell within a cell cluster is non-zero, other cells in the cluster must balance it by force transmission through cell-cell adhesions.
source: Following from this, if the integrated traction force over the footprint of an individual cell within a cell cluster is non-zero, other cells in the cluster must balance it by force transmission through cell–cell adhesions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the force-balancing principle.

claim: The residual traction force for a particular cell within a cluster determines the vectorial sum of external forces this cell experiences through cell-cell adhesions.
source: Thus, the residual traction force for a particular cell within a cluster determines the vectorial sum of external forces this cell experiences through cell–cell adhesions (Equation 1 in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a logical inference from the force-balancing principle.

claim: The median error of force calculations based on the force-balancing principle was approximately 14% of the expected force magnitudes.
source: Statistical analyses of our experimental data indicate that the median error of force calculations based on the force-balancing principle was ∼14% of the expected force magnitudes (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both the force-balancing approach and the FEM approach yielded consistent results for cell-cell forces in tree-like topologies.
source: Our analyses indicated that both approaches yielded consistent results; the error for interface force calculations by the FEM approach is comparable to the error we found for force calculations by the force balancing principle alone (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inaccuracy in FEM-predicted forces arises from the same sources of error as the inaccuracy in force balance-predicted forces, which are uncertainties in the traction force reconstruction.
source: This implies that the inaccuracy in FEM-predicted forces arises from the same sources of error as the inaccuracy in force balance-predicted forces, which are uncertainties in the traction force reconstruction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of the two methods.

claim: Neither the simplifying approximation of the cell cluster by a homogeneous thin-plate nor the numerical solution of the model introduced substantial error when predicting cell-cell forces in tree-like topologies.
source: Thus, neither the simplifying approximation of the cell cluster by a homogeneous thin-plate nor the numerical solution of the model introduced substantial error when predicting cell–cell forces in 'tree-like' topologies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation analysis comparing FEM and force-balancing methods.

claim: As a cell in a cluster entered mitosis, the overall mechanical energy deposited into the substrate by either the entire cluster or the dividing cell transiently decreased.
source: We found that, as a cell in a cluster entered mitosis, the overall mechanical energy deposited into the substrate by either the entire cluster or the dividing cell transiently decreased (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The drop in strain energy during mitosis reflected the detachment of the dividing cell from the cell-matrix as it became rounded.
source: The drop in strain energy during mitosis reflected the detachment of the dividing cell from the cell–matrix as it became rounded (Video 4), consistent with previous assertions (Terasima and Tolmach, 1963; Burton and Taylor, 1997; Tanimoto and Sano, 2012).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by observations in Video 4 and citations to previous literature.

claim: Each mitotic event correlated with a dramatic decrease in the forces which the dividing cell exchanged with its neighbors.
source: Each mitotic event correlated with a dramatic decrease in the forces, which the dividing cell exchanged with its neighbors (Figure 4F–H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Mitosis is accompanied by weakening of not only cell-matrix adhesions but also cell-cell adhesions.
source: Each mitotic event correlated with a dramatic decrease in the forces, which the dividing cell exchanged with its neighbors (Figure 4F–H), suggesting that mitosis is accompanied by weakening of not only cell–matrix adhesions but also cell–cell adhesions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in forces during mitosis.

claim: During mitotic events, the sum of cell-cell force magnitudes over all junctions in the cell cluster remained constant before increasing to a higher plateau value.
source: Interestingly, during mitotic events, the sum of cell–cell force magnitudes over all junctions in the cell cluster remained constant before increasing to a higher plateau value (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The loss of cell-cell forces at the junctions of the dividing cell was balanced at other junctions in the cluster.
source: This suggested that the loss of cell–cell forces at the junctions of the dividing cell was balanced at other junctions in the cluster (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that total cluster forces remain constant during mitosis.

claim: During major morphological changes, force fluctuations at individual cell-cell junctions can be dynamically compensated by forces at other cell junctions.
source: These results show that, during major morphological changes, force fluctuations at individual cell–cell junctions can be dynamically compensated by forces at other cell junctions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mitosis experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: A positive and statistically significant correlation was observed between E-cadherin-GFP intensities integrated along each cell-cell junction and the force measured for each junction.
source: We correlated the E-cadherin-GFP intensities integrated along each cell–cell junction with the force measured for each junction and observed a positive and statistically significant correlation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The positive correlation between E-cadherin intensity and force persisted on a stiffer matrix.
source: The positive correlation also persisted on a stiffer matrix (Figure 5A), indicating that the overall relation between force exchange and E-cadherin recruitment is robust and independent of substrate compliance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on different substrate stiffnesses shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The overall relation between force exchange and E-cadherin recruitment is robust and independent of substrate compliance.
source: The positive correlation also persisted on a stiffer matrix (Figure 5A), indicating that the overall relation between force exchange and E-cadherin recruitment is robust and independent of substrate compliance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the correlation persists across different substrate stiffnesses.

claim: Function-blocking antibodies targeting E-cadherin resulted in a significant reduction in cell-cell force measurements.
source: We further validated the central role of cadherin proteins in mediating cell–cell force transmission by using function-blocking antibodies targeting E-cadherin directly (Petrova et al., 2012) or by knock-down of alpha-catenin, an essential adaptor protein of cadherin-mediated adhesions (Yonemura et al., 2010). Both perturbations resulted in a significant reduction in cell–cell force measurements (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental perturbation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knock-down of alpha-catenin resulted in a significant reduction in cell-cell force measurements.
source: We further validated the central role of cadherin proteins in mediating cell–cell force transmission by using function-blocking antibodies targeting E-cadherin directly (Petrova et al., 2012) or by knock-down of alpha-catenin, an essential adaptor protein of cadherin-mediated adhesions (Yonemura et al., 2010). Both perturbations resulted in a significant reduction in cell–cell force measurements (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental perturbation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The junctional recruitment of E-cadherin is coupled to the cell-cell adhesion forces.
source: These results support the model that the junctional recruitment of E-cadherin is coupled to the cell–cell adhesion forces (Liu et al., 2010; Borghi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the correlation and perturbation experiments, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: A positive and statistically significant correlation exists between local E-cadherin-GFP intensities and cell-cell stress measurements.
source: Indeed, this visual impression could be confirmed quantitatively by a positive and statistically significant correlation between local E-cadherin-GFP intensities and cell–cell stress measurements (Figure 6B), both on soft and stiff substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The length scale over which cell-cell stresses and E-cadherin intensity are coupled is 9.6 µm on 8 kPa substrates.
source: We found this length to be 9.6 µm (Figure 6C) or 12.8 µm (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) depending on whether the cells were cultured on soft (8 kPa) or stiff (35 kPa) substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by randomization analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The length scale over which cell-cell stresses and E-cadherin intensity are coupled is 12.8 µm on 35 kPa substrates.
source: We found this length to be 9.6 µm (Figure 6C) or 12.8 µm (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) depending on whether the cells were cultured on soft (8 kPa) or stiff (35 kPa) substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by randomization analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The length scale of force-E-cadherin coupling is consistent with the length scale over which E-cadherin-GFP proteins are modulated along cell-cell junctions, which was measured to be 13 µm based on autocorrelation.
source: This length scale is consistent with the length scale over which E-cadherin-GFP proteins are modulated along cell–cell junctions in our system, which we measured to be 13 µm based on autocorrelation of E-cadherin-GFP intensities along the cell junctions (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The measured length scale of force-E-cadherin coupling is likely related to the spatial organization of E-cadherin along the cell-cell junctions and not a resolution limit of the FEM analysis.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the measured length scale of force–E-cadherin coupling is likely related to the spatial organization of E-cadherin along the cell–cell junctions and not a resolution limit of the FEM analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of the coupling length scale with the E-cadherin autocorrelation length scale.

claim: The median as well as the entire distribution of correlations between local cell-cell stress magnitudes and E-cadherin-GFP intensities increased with junction length.
source: Indeed, we found that the median as well as the entire distribution of correlations between local cell–cell stress magnitudes and E-cadherin-GFP intensities increased with junction length (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The results are consistent with reports that mechanical forces exerted by actomyosin contractility are critical for junction growth and maturation.
source: These results are consistent with more qualitative reports that mechanical forces exerted by actomyosin contractility are critical for junction growth and maturation (Shewan et al., 2005; Yamada and Nelson, 2007; Borghi et al., 2012; Brieher and Yap, 2013).
evidence: This claim relates the findings to previous literature.

claim: When junctions were re-established after mitosis, those embedded in the cell cluster had lower force transmission compared to junctions at the cluster periphery.
source: When junctions were re-established after mitosis, those embedded in the cell cluster had lower force transmission compared to junctions at the cluster periphery (network in Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: With increasing degree of connectivity (k), the sum of cell-cell forces increased.
source: With increasing k, the sum of cell–cell forces increased (Figure 7A), which indicates that the cumulative force a cell experiences through its cell–cell adhesions increases with the number of connected neighbors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The cumulative force a cell experiences through its cell-cell adhesions increases with the number of connected neighbors.
source: With increasing k, the sum of cell–cell forces increased (Figure 7A), which indicates that the cumulative force a cell experiences through its cell–cell adhesions increases with the number of connected neighbors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that sum of cell-cell forces increases with k.

claim: The increase in cumulative cell-cell forces for higher k-values was not paralleled by stronger cell-matrix traction forces.
source: Strikingly, the increase in cumulative cell–cell forces for higher k-values was not paralleled by stronger cell–matrix traction forces (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The generation and exchange of forces at cell-cell junctions can be decoupled from cell-matrix traction force generation, especially in larger cell clusters where cells have higher k values.
source: Thus, contrary to the conclusions drawn from examining cell doublets (Maruthamuthu et al., 2011), the generation and exchange of forces at cell–cell junctions can be decoupled from cell–matrix traction force generation, especially in larger cell clusters where cells have higher k values.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cell-cell forces increase with k while traction forces do not.

claim: Focal adhesions and traction forces are primarily localized at the periphery of cell clusters.
source: This result is further supported by the observation that focal adhesions and traction forces are primarily localized at the periphery of cell clusters (Figure 8), consistent with a previous report (Mertz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 8 and a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells on stiffer (35 kPa) substrates exerted higher traction forces compared to cells on softer (8 kPa) substrates.
source: In general, cells on stiffer (35 kPa) substrates exerted higher traction forces compared to cells on softer (8 kPa) substrates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: On 8 kPa substrates, cell-cell forces at individual junctions were independent of the minimal k values.
source: On 8 kPa substrates, cell–cell forces at individual junctions were independent of the minimal k values (Figure 7C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: On 8 kPa substrates, cell-cell stresses increased for junctions with higher minimal k values.
source: On 8 kPa substrates, cell–cell forces at individual junctions were independent of the minimal k values (Figure 7C), whereas the cell–cell stresses, calculated by normalizing cell–cell force to junction length, increased for junctions with higher minimal k values (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The stresses exerted between cells are higher towards the center of epithelial sheets.
source: This is consistent with a previous analysis of cellular stresses in epithelial sheets, in which the stresses exerted between cells were proposed to be higher towards the center of the sheet (Trepat et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim references a previous study.

claim: On 35 kPa substrates, the forces as well as stresses exerted on individual cell-cell junctions decreased with increasing minimal k of the junction.
source: In contrast, on 35 kPa substrates, the forces as well as stresses exerted on individual cell–cell junctions decreased with increasing minimal k of the junction (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: For cell clusters on the stiffer substrate, the cell-cell forces were transmitted predominantly between cluster-peripheral cells and not across the cluster center.
source: Hence, for cell clusters on the stiffer substrate, the cell–cell forces were transmitted predominantly between cluster-peripheral cells and not across the cluster center.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that forces decrease with minimal k on stiff substrates.

claim: The spatial pattern of cell-cell force transmission is modulated by the mechanical microenvironment.
source: Thus, the spatial pattern of cell–cell force transmission is modulated by the mechanical microenvironment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the different force patterns observed on different substrate stiffnesses.

claim: For control MCF10A cells, the coupling between cell-cell forces and cell-matrix was stronger than the coupling between cell-cell forces at opposing cell junctions, irrespective of substrate stiffness.
source: For control MCF10A cells, the coupling between cell–cell forces and cell–matrix was stronger than the coupling between cell–cell forces at opposing cell junctions, irrespective of substrate stiffness (Figure 9B)
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Forces exerted at cell-cell junctions were only weakly transmitted through a cell.
source: For control MCF10A cells, the coupling between cell–cell forces and cell–matrix was stronger than the coupling between cell–cell forces at opposing cell junctions, irrespective of substrate stiffness (Figure 9B), indicating that forces exerted at cell–cell junctions were only weakly transmitted through a cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Long-range force transmission is an active process where forces exerted on a cell activate signaling pathways and contractile machineries that are responsible for transducing force to neighboring cells.
source: However, our data could be reconciled with this observation if long-range force transmission is an active process: forces exerted on a cell activate signaling pathways and contractile machineries that are responsible for transducing force to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to reconcile the findings with previous observations.

claim: Each individual cell in a cell cluster, though linked with one another, functions independently with the ability to promote or attenuate force transduction.
source: In this model, each individual cell in a cell cluster, though linked with one another, functions independently with the ability to promote or attenuate force transduction.
evidence: This is part of the speculative model proposed.

claim: Forces at cell-cell junctions may be transmitted to the substrate via cell-matrix adhesions, thus intercepting the mechanical link between opposing cell-cell junctions (force anchoring mechanism).
source: There are two non-exclusive mechanisms that could attenuate force transduction across individual cells: first, forces at cell–cell junctions may be transmitted to the substrate via cell–matrix adhesions, thus intercepting the mechanical link between opposing cell–cell junctions ('force anchoring mechanism').
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observations.

claim: Each cell may have a basal actomyosin contractility level that is autonomous from extracellular force stimuli and high enough to overcome the cell-external forces (force scrambling mechanism).
source: Second, each cell may have a basal actomyosin contractility level that is autonomous from extracellular force stimuli and high enough to overcome the cell-external forces ('force scrambling mechanism').
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observations.

claim: The traction forces exerted by cells with reduced paxillin or talin-1 were significantly lower than the traction forces of control cells.
source: Indeed, the traction forces exerted by cells with reduced paxillin or talin-1 were significantly lower than the traction forces of control cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D,H.

claim: In cell pairs in which both cells had paxillin downregulated, forces at the cell-cell junction were unchanged compared to control cell pairs.
source: In cell pairs in which both cells had paxillin downregulated, forces at the cell–cell junction were unchanged compared to control cell pairs, indicating that paxillin knock-down did not affect cell–cell force transmission (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Paxillin knock-down did not affect cell-cell force transmission.
source: In cell pairs in which both cells had paxillin downregulated, forces at the cell–cell junction were unchanged compared to control cell pairs, indicating that paxillin knock-down did not affect cell–cell force transmission (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cell-cell forces were unchanged in paxillin-downregulated cell pairs.

claim: In talin-1-downregulated cell pairs, cell-cell forces were lower than those of control cell pairs.
source: In talin-1-downregulated cell pairs, although cell–cell forces were lower than those of control cell pairs, cell–cell junction morphology was unaffected, and cell–cell force transmission was restored almost to control levels when the talin-1 downregulated cells were embedded in larger clusters (Figure 9—figure supplement 1F,G,M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Cell-cell force transmission was restored almost to control levels when talin-1 downregulated cells were embedded in larger clusters.
source: In talin-1-downregulated cell pairs, although cell–cell forces were lower than those of control cell pairs, cell–cell junction morphology was unaffected, and cell–cell force transmission was restored almost to control levels when the talin-1 downregulated cells were embedded in larger clusters (Figure 9—figure supplement 1F,G,M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1M.

claim: The correlation between the fluctuations of cell-cell forces in opposing junctions of a paxillin or talin-1 downregulated cell was higher than that between the cell-cell force fluctuations in opposing junctions of control cells.
source: Importantly, the correlation between the fluctuations of cell–cell forces in opposing junctions of a paxillin or talin-1 downregulated cell was higher than that between the cell–cell force fluctuations in opposing junctions of control cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: For talin-1 downregulated cells, the correlation between the fluctuations of cell-cell forces in opposing junctions was higher than that between the cell-cell force and traction force fluctuations.
source: For talin-1 downregulated cells, which exert very low traction forces (Figure 9—figure supplement 1H), the correlation between the fluctuations of cell–cell forces in opposing junctions was in addition higher than that between the cell–cell force and traction force fluctuations (Figure 9B,D–E; Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B,D-E.

claim: The decoupling from the matrix of a cell within a cluster promotes the transmission of forces across the cell, from one cell-cell junction to the next, in support of the force anchoring mechanism.
source: These data showed that the decoupling from the matrix of a cell within a cluster promotes the transmission of forces across the cell, from one cell–cell junction to the next, in support of the force anchoring mechanism as one way a cell may attenuate long-range force transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the perturbation experiments with paxillin and talin-1 downregulation.

claim: In cell pairs in which both cells had downregulated myosin-IIA, the traction forces exerted by the cells, as well as the forces exerted through the cell-cell junctions, were significantly decreased.
source: In cell pairs in which both cells had downregulated myosin-IIA, the traction forces exerted by the cells, as well as the forces exerted through the cell–cell junctions, were significantly decreased (Figure 9—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1K-L.

claim: Cells with downregulated myosin-IIA exerted forces at their cell-cell junctions close to control levels when embedded in larger clusters.
source: Although myosin-IIA downregulation affected cell–cell and cell–matrix mechanotransduction, cell–cell junctions were still able to form in cell clusters, as the cell–cell junction morphology of myosin-IIA downregulated cells remained similar to control cells and cells with downregulated myosin-IIA exerted forces at their cell–cell junctions close to control levels when embedded in larger clusters (Figure 9—figure supplement 1J,N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1N.

claim: Cells with myosin-IIA knock-down showed a significant increase in the correlation of force fluctuations at opposing junctions compared to control cells.
source: As with talin-1 downregulated cells, cells with myosin-IIA knock-down showed a significant increase in the correlation of force fluctuations at opposing junctions compared to control cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Cells with reduced actomyosin contractility act as passive force transducers between other contractile cells in a cluster, consistent with the force scrambling mechanism.
source: This shows that cells with reduced actomyosin contractility act as passive force transducers between other contractile cells in a cluster, consistent with the force scrambling mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the myosin-IIA downregulation experiments.

claim: Force fluctuations at individual cell-cell junctions can be dynamically compensated by forces at other cell junctions to maintain mechanical stress homeostasis.
source: These results show that, during major morphological changes, force fluctuations at individual cell–cell junctions can be dynamically compensated by forces at other cell junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that total cluster forces remain constant during mitosis while individual junction forces change.

claim: The method can resolve cell-cell forces at a length scale of approximately 10 micrometers.
source: We found this length to be 9.6 µm (Figure 6C) or 12.8 µm (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) depending on whether the cells were cultured on soft (8 kPa) or stiff (35 kPa) substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the coupling length scale between forces and E-cadherin.
